metadata.document_title: Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Hypertension in Adults: Diagnostic Cutoffs, Drug Classes, and Management Algorithms

sections.section_title: Hypertension Diagnostic Criteria and Blood Pressure Staging
sections.text: Hypertension is diagnosed when on two different days, the systolic blood pressure readings on both days are >= 140 mmHg and/or the diastolic blood pressure readings on both days are >= 90 mmHg. Standard blood pressure classifications are defined as: Normal Blood Pressure: Systolic < 120 mmHg and Diastolic < 80 mmHg; Elevated Blood Pressure: Systolic 120-129 mmHg and Diastolic < 80 mmHg; Stage 1 Hypertension: Systolic 130-139 mmHg or Diastolic 80-89 mmHg; Stage 2 Hypertension: Systolic >= 140 mmHg or Diastolic >= 90 mmHg; Hypertensive Crisis: Systolic > 180 mmHg and/or Diastolic > 120 mmHg. WHO recommends pharmacological antihypertensive treatment initiation for individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension of systolic blood pressure >= 140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >= 90 mmHg.

The World Health Organization recommends initiation of treatment with any of the three classes of first-line antihypertensive medications: 1. Thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics (e.g., Chlorthalidone 12.5-25 mg daily, Hydrochlorothiazide 25-50 mg daily); 2. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, e.g., Lisinopril 10-40 mg daily, Enalapril 5-20 mg daily) or Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs, e.g., Losartan 50-100 mg daily, Telmisartan 40-80 mg daily); 3. Long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs, e.g., Amlodipine 5-10 mg daily). Combination therapy, preferably with a single-pill fixed-dose combination, is recommended as initial treatment when baseline blood pressure is >= 20/10 mmHg above target.

sections.section_title: Critical Medication Contraindications and Safety Warnings
sections.text: ACE inhibitors and ARBs must NOT be combined simultaneously in the treatment of hypertension. Dual renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockade significantly increases the clinical risk of hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury (renal impairment), and symptomatic hypotension without providing additional cardiovascular mortality benefit. In addition, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to fetal renal dysgenesis and teratogenicity. Calcium channel blockers are preferred in patients with bronchial asthma or isolated systolic hypertension, while beta-blockers are not recommended as first-line therapy for uncomplicated primary hypertension unless specific compelling indications exist such as angina, post-myocardial infarction, or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

Lifestyle modifications are essential non-pharmacological interventions recommended for all individuals with elevated blood pressure or hypertension. Key interventions include: 1. Dietary sodium restriction: reduce daily sodium intake to less than 2,000 mg/day (equivalent to approximately 5 g/day of salt); 2. Healthy dietary patterns: adoption of the DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension), rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, nuts, and low-fat dairy while minimizing saturated fats; 3. Regular physical activity: at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week; 4. Weight reduction: maintenance of a healthy body mass index (BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2); 5. Tobacco cessation and alcohol restriction.

sections.section_title: Blood Pressure Targets and Follow-up Frequency
sections.text: For adults with uncomplicated hypertension receiving pharmacological therapy, WHO recommends a target blood pressure of < 140/90 mmHg. In individuals with established cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or diabetes mellitus, a lower blood pressure target of < 130/80 mmHg is recommended. Following the initiation or modification of antihypertensive medications, patient blood pressure should be re-evaluated every 2 to 4 weeks until target levels are consistently achieved, followed by routine follow-up assessments every 3 to 6 months.
